Groundwater availability is closely related to the type of underlying bedrock. The Martinsburg Formation is considered to have poor groundwater availability. Yields range from 10 to 50 gallons per minute (gpm) with two to five gpm per foot of drawdown.
Carbonate rocks are generally excellent sources of groundwater yielding in excess of 300 gpm with 25 gpm per foot of drawdown.
Usage of groundwater for private water supplies is generally believed to be diminishing with urban expansion.
The effect of Tropical Storm Agnes and its floodwaters on groundwater in the Harrisburg area is not known except for the abundant recharge to the aquifers. No reports have been received regarding a noticeable permanent change in water table elevation or in the general quality of the groundwater.
Seasonal variation in water table elevations will continue to occur with periodic sharp increases due to storm rainfall. As neither the nature of the terrain nor the water supply of Dauphin County is affected by groundwater, no change in conditions is projected with or without the project.
f. Climatology
The climate of Harrisburg is humid with moderate winters. Excessive precipitation is relatively infrequent with the heaviest rainfall usually occurring during the summer months. Mean annual precipitation is 37.6 inches.
The longest period with maximum temperature 90° F and above was 17 days in July and August, 1941. Winters are modified by the presence of the Blue Mountains. Mean annual snowfall is in the order of 36 inches and generally occurs in November through March. Traces are generally recorded in April, and some have been recorded in October. A minimum daily temperature of 32° F or less was recorded consecutively for 60 days (1944-1945), while the longest spell of zero degrees or below was four days in January, 1936.
